Egg diameter in European minnow Phoxinus phoxinus has been measured at approximately 0.016 centimeters  under the thermal regime characteristic of Lake Windermere, where the long-term mean water temperature from 1933 to 1975 was 10.25 °C [T = 10.25 °C]. Newly fertilised ova are demersal and adhesive, adhering to gravel substrates until eclosion. At this same ambient temperature, the prolarvae emerge from the chorion at a fork length of roughly 0.5 centimeters [Lb = roughly 0.5 centimeters], a size that reflects the modest yolk reserves provisioned within at a temperature of 10.25 °C [T = 10.25 °C]each egg. The transition from yolk-sac larva to actively feeding juvenile, marked by the disappearance of the yolk sac, occurs approximately 14 days after hatching  when individuals reach a fork length of about 0.8 centimeters [Lj = ab at a temperature of 10.25 °C [T = 10.25 °C] at a temperature of 10.25 °C [T = 10.25 °C]out 0.8 centimeters]. This metamorphic milestone signals the onset of exogenous feeding and a shift from a lecithotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition, during which the larvae begin foraging for zooplankton.

The ultimate total length attained by Phoxinus phoxinus has been documented at 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], representing the maximum fork length observed in wild populations. This asymptotic size is considerably smaller than that of many other cyprinids inhabiting similar Palearctic waters, a pattern that likely reflects the species’ adaptation to cold, unproductive streams and lakes where growth rates are constrained by short growing seasons and limited food availability. Body mass at this terminal length, estimated from length–weight regressions derived from the literature, reaches approximately 29 grams [Wwi = approximately 29 grams] in fully grown adults. In contrast, the mean wet weight of a sample of 34 freshly caught individuals from Sec Lake in Spain, measuring between 4.8 and 8.6 centimeters in standard length, was recorded as 5.38 grams , a value that integrates both juvenile and adult contributions. A parallel measurement from the same collection yielded an identical mean wet weight of 5.38 grams , confirming the consistency of the sample.

Sexual maturation in the European minnow is reached at a fork length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a relatively modest size that allows individuals to begin reproducing within their first or second summer. The time elapsed from hatching to this pubertal milestone, as recorded under a mean water temperature of 11.4 °C [T = 11.4 °C], is approximately 137 days after hatching [tp = approximately 137 days after hatching]. This rapid attainment of reproductive maturity is characteristic of a species that inhabits ephemeral or seasonally challenging environments where early investment in reproduction confers a selective advantage. Newly hatched larvae, upon eclosion, have a wet weight of approximately 0.00181 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00181 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous yolk reserves that must sustain them through the brief lecithotrophic phase. The wet weight of the freshly spawned egg, measured at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is about 0.00334 grams [Ww0 = about 0.00334 grams], representing the initial maternal investment per offspring.

Experimental rearing trials have quantified the thermal sensitivity of embryonic development in Phoxinus phoxinus across a broad temperature gradient. At 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C], the incubation period until hatching averages 9.9 days , whereas at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] this duration shortens to 5.9 days . Further increases to 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C] yield a hatching time of 6 days , while at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] the value is 5 days . Warmer temperatures accelerate development considerably: eggs incubated at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] hatch after only 3.9 days , and at the highest tested temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] eclosion occurs in a remarkably brief 2.5 days . This pronounced thermal dependency underscores the species’ capacity to adjust its embryonic timing in response to local thermal regimes, a critical adaptation in the variable headwater streams it occupies. The mass-specific resting metabolic rate of this species, measured at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is 0.22 milliliters of oxygen per hour per gram , a value consistent with the relatively low basal metabolic demands of a small-bodied, cold-water cyprinid.

Longevity records for Phoxinus phoxinus in the wild indicate a maximum lifespan of up to 13 years [am = up to 13 years] under the cold thermal conditions characteristic of the River Hinogla, the outlet of Lake Ovre Heimdalsvatn in Norway, where the mean surface water temperature is 3.79 °C [T = 3.79 °C]. This extended lifespan, unusually high for a cyprinid of such small body size, is likely linked to the extremely slow metabolic rates imposed by the near-freezing waters. Reproductive output under these same frigid conditions, at a temperature of 3.79 °C [T = 3.79 °C], has been estimated at approximately 1000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1000 eggs per year], produced in a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = a single spawning event per year], reflecting a relatively low annual fecundity that is compensated by iteroparity over many years. The time to first reproduction from hatching under a mean temperature of 11.4 °C [T = 11.4 °C] was recorded as 137 days after hatching [tR = 137 days after hatching], confirming the tight coupling between thermal regime and life-history scheduling in this species. Collectively, these data paint a portrait of a small, cold-adapted cyprinid that balances rapid juvenile development with a remarkably long adult lifespan, an unusual combination among freshwater teleosts.
